How to Stay Invested During Market Volatility
article:
If you’ve opened your brokerage app lately, swallowed hard, and closed it immediately, you’re not alone.
Watching red numbers flash across your screen is enough to give anyone a knot in their stomach.
Whether it’s sticky global inflation, shifting central bank
interest rate
policies, escalating Middle East
geopolitical tension
, or unexpected corporate earnings hiccups, market turbulence has a habit of making us feel like the ground under our feet is shaking.
In moments like these, the urge to smash the “sell all” button and hide under the covers with cold hard cash feels almost primal.
Here’s the catch: jumping out of moving cars usually ends poorly, and jumping out of the stock market mid-storm is no different.
Volatility Isn’t a Bug – It’s a Feature
It’s easy to confuse a drop in share price with a drop in real-world business value.
But stock markets aren’t always rational short-term price tags; they behave more like moody crowds.
When
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, sees its share price dip during a market sell-off, it rarely means depositors have stopped saving or home buyers have stopped servicing their mortgages overnight.
Similarly, when
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68), or SGX, experiences short-term price pressure, it doesn’t mean investors and institutions have ceased trading equities and derivatives on the local bourse.
Short-term price swings reflect market sentiment, not necessarily a fundamental breakdown in balance sheets or earnings potential.
Historically, market corrections (drops of 10% or more) happen every couple of years, and bear markets are a regular part of economic cycles.
Selling in a panic turns temporary paper losses into permanent, real losses.
Worse, you force yourself to solve an almost impossible puzzle: guessing the exact day to buy back in.
Verified historical market data shows that missing just a handful of the market’s best single-day recovery leaps – which frequently occur during or right after major downturns – can decimate your total portfolio returns over a 10- or 20-year horizon.
Related articles:
Singapore Bank Shares Have Fallen. Are They Cheap Enough Yet?
3 Dividend Blue Chips Powering the STI’s 2026 Rally
Focus on the Business, Not the Price Ticker
Staying invested doesn’t mean wearing blinders.
It means shifting your focus from fluctuating stock charts to core business metrics: net profit margins, free cash flow, debt-servicing ability, and durable competitive moats.
A falling share price in a solid
blue chip
is often just a temporary sale.
However, staying the course doesn’t mean holding every single business indefinitely.
There’s a big difference between a temporary cyclical slump and a structural decline.
If a company is saddled with unsustainable debt, suffering from deteriorating margins, or losing ground to competitors, it may be time to cut your losses.
But if the core engine of the business remains sound, short-term noise is just that –
noise
.
Sleep Soundly: Build a Downturn-Proof Portfolio
If a market dip keeps you awake at night, your portfolio is likely out of sync with your personal risk tolerance.
Diversify wisely:
Don’t put all your eggs in one basket. Balancing steady Singapore dividend-paying anchors and resilient
real estate investment trusts (REITs)
like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, with global tech or
growth equities
helps smooth out wild localised swings.
Keep cash on hand:
Never invest money you’ll need for next month’s mortgage or emergency bills. Having a robust cash cushion prevents you from being forced to sell depressed assets to pay for life’s unexpected expenses.
Related articles:
The “Sleep Well at Night” Portfolio: 4 SGX Stocks That Thrive in Market Chaos
Looking for Income? 4 Singapore Stocks That Pay You While You Sleep
Put Volatility to Work
Instead of fearing volatility, use it.
Dollar-cost averaging (DCA):
Consistently putting a set amount of money into the market at regular intervals automatically buys you more units when prices are down and fewer when prices are high. It takes the guesswork out of deciding when to invest.
Shop for quality:
Market panics regularly dump great companies into the bargain bin. Assess valuations carefully and treat pullbacks as chances to acquire income-generating assets at higher distribution yields.
Don’t try to catch falling knives:
Trying to call the exact market bottom is a fool’s errand. Focus on acquiring good businesses at fair prices rather than waiting for an elusive “perfect bottom”.
Control the Only Thing You Can: Your Behaviour
Panicked decisions are rarely smart decisions.
One of the best practical moves you can make during a volatile market is simple: stop checking your portfolio every day.
Constant monitoring magnifies anxiety and triggers impulsive trades.
Set clear rules for yourself: define your buying, selling, and asset allocation parameters before emotional headlines hit the newsstands.
Think in Years, Not Days
Wealth creation isn’t built over a frantic afternoon of trading; it compounds steadily over decades.
Reinvesting dividend payouts during down periods lets you accumulate more shares that will work harder for you when the economic tide inevitably turns back up.
Remember why you started this journey in the first place – whether it’s funding your children’s tertiary education, securing a comfortable retirement, or building a passive income stream for your family.
A temporary market blip doesn’t change your long-term life goals.
Related articles:
Starting at Primary 1: The Impact of a 15-Year Dividend Compounding Journey
What I Would Buy Today to Build a Retirement Income Portfolio from Scratch
Get Smart: Stay Calm, Stay Disciplined, Stay Invested
Market downturns are uncomfortable, but they are inevitable.
Success over time isn’t about avoiding every single market drop.
It’s about building a disciplined, diversified strategy that lets you
navigate the storm calmly
without abandoning your financial destination.
Keep monitoring company balance sheets, keep your cash buffer intact, and let time and
compounding
do the heavy lifting for you.

title: China plans AI tech export curbs to manage security risks
article:
(Oct 16): China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to keep closer control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector.

The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds.

Chinese AI startups have this summer made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s latest editions offer better pricing and Chinese companies also favour the approach of sharing the weights — used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer — of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They’re also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI Co making their wares available on US cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services.

The proposed export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of AI technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defence industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities.

“The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models containing at least two trillion parameters — like Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s Qwen3.8-Max — or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. The curb would cover model weights, checkpoints, source code and architecture.

See also: China looks to tighten biotech exports, allows licensing deals

The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licensing regime and potential US sanctions. The proposed restrictions against shipping mega-parameter models abroad are likely to hamper development given AI labs are training ever larger platforms: just last month, Alibaba declared plans to develop models with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, far larger than what’s common today, for longer and more complex tasks.

AI models trained on China’s “core data”, as defined by relevant legislation such as the Data Security Law, will be banned from export, according to the proposal. The Data Security Law describes state core data as “data concerning national security, the lifeline of the national economy, key public livelihoods, and major public interests”.

Open-source technology and research already in the public domain wouldn’t be covered, and the government will provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Beijing said the measures weren’t aimed at any particular country, region or entity.

See also: China’s payback for late stimulus looms with sub-4.5% growth

China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect Friday and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licensing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control.

Deploying a covered model overseas would constitute a technology export, according to a statement. Deployments on overseas infrastructure owned by the Chinese provider could qualify for automatic licensing.

title: China looks to tighten biotech exports, allows licensing deals
article:
(Oct 16): China is looking to tighten biotechnology exports, but will leave the door open for licensing deals with foreign drugmakers that have underpinned its position as a growing pharmaceutical powerhouse.

Beijing is proposing to add five biomedical technologies to its export-control list, according to a statement from the Ministry of Commerce. The draft proposal, released Friday, includes two types of cutting-edge medical technology platforms to treat diseases at a genetic level. But the list clarifies that restrictions don’t apply to licensing, partnerships and contract research services involving these technologies.

Multinational pharmaceutical companies are increasingly rushing to secure global licensing deals for experimental drugs developed by Chinese companies. There were 81 licensing deals worth up to US$110 billion ($141 billion) in the first half of 2026 — on track to surpass last year’s record, according to government statistics.

Allowing licensing deals will provide some relief for the pharmaceutical industry globally. US and European firms say China’s deep pipeline of drug candidates means more innovative drugs with big sales potential. For Chinese drugmakers, the deals offer cash and international recognition — crucial to China’s goal of becoming a global leader in biomedical research.

The growing frequency and prominence of the collaborations have become a source of tension between the US and China in recent years. Some US lawmakers and investors have called for more restrictions on such deals to protect the American biotech industry.

The US Treasury Department is expected to release new regulations this year that could subject biotech licensing deals to the same outbound investment reviews as semiconductors and artificial intelligence systems.

See also: China’s payback for late stimulus looms with sub-4.5% growth

China’s proposed export controls on ownership transfer focus on small interfering RNA molecules that can silence disease-causing genes, as well as cell and gene therapies that have the potential to treat conditions from cancer to rare disease. The restrictions also cover research and technologies related to disease-causing microorganisms.

In addition to the biomedical sector, China outlined plans to control exports in artificial intelligence and solar energy technologies.

title: China buys more US soybeans as purchasing spree gathers pace — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 16): China has purchased more cargoes of US soybeans, extending a buying spree this week that marks its first acquisitions since the leaders of the two countries held a summit in late September.

State-owned companies have booked at least 20 soybean shipments that will be delivered from the US Gulf and Pacific West, according to people familiar with the matter, equivalent to around 1.3 million tonnes. Cargoes will be mainly loaded from December to March, they said, asking not to be named as they’re not authorised to speak to the media.

The US Department of Agriculture announced 800,000 tonnes of soybean sales to China in spot reports this week, equivalent to about 12 cargoes, for delivery in the 2026-27 marketing year. The agency also reported the sale of 283,450 tonnes to unknown destinations, some of which could end up in the Asian nation.

Beijing is set to reduce duties on a range of US agricultural products including wheat and corn, according to lists released by the countries after the summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. The cuts are part of a plan to lower tariffs on about US$30 billion of imports from each nation.

Soybeans, however, have been left off the duty reduction lists so far and US cargoes coming to China would still incur about 13% tariffs, making the trade unviable for commercial buyers. State-owned firms are largely driving the trade, as Beijing makes steady progress to fulfill a pledge to buy at least 25 million tonnes of American soybeans annually through 2028.

title: Deluge closes at 64 cents on first day of trading; reaches intra-day high of 65 cents
article:
Fire detection and protection system contractor Deluge Corporation Limited (Deluge) closed at 64 cents on its first day of trading on Oct 16, valuing the company at $92.8 million.

Deluge’s share price debuted at 63 cents, 5% higher from its initial public offering (IPO) price of 60 cents, and reached an intra-day high of 65 cents. At the close of trading on Oct 16, more than 8.7 million shares changed hands.

On Oct 15, Deluge announced that its IPO was 3.86 times subscribed, with the public tranche being nearly 12 times subscribed while the placement tranche being 3.42 times subscribed.

Maybank Securities and SAC Capital are the joint bookrunners and underwriters for the offering.

title: Taiwan to fund US$4 bil Texas industrial complex for AI, Nvidia partners
article:
(Oct 16): Taiwan plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US that would build a base for a comprehensive supply chain for Nvidia Corp and other artificial intelligence (AI) hardware makers in the country.

The initiative is starting with a complex in Texas that would cost as much as US$4 billion to build, according to Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin. The facilities would help smaller suppliers that are essential to the operations of Nvidia’s main production partner Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) and AI server assemblers including Foxconn Technology Group to set up shop in the US, Kung said.

Each complex would run between US$2 billion and US$4 billion to build, and the government is planning “more than one” site on US soil, Kung said in an Oct 12 interview with Bloomberg News. The Taiwanese government is partnering with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association, which will be responsible for raising required funding to develop the complexes, he said.

“We are going to establish a long-term, sustainable supply chain there that can also be joined by American firms and local workers, and not just Taiwanese companies,” Kung said.

Companies like TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron Corp provide essential hardware for data centers and are critical to the success of US AI chipmakers including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc, and cloud service providers such as Meta Platforms Inc and Microsoft Corp. These Taiwanese manufacturing titans depend in turn on lesser-known partners that make a wide range of parts from chip packaging substrates to cooling modules — everything that’s required in an AI data centre.

But while TSMC and Foxconn are capable of funding and managing their own US expansion, that’s not always the case for smaller firms. That’s how Taiwan is hoping the new industrial complexes in the US could help.

See also: Toyota to debut its own version of Tesla EV-making tech in China

Many of these suppliers got a boost from Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang when he cited the names of a few dozen parts makers during a keynote presentation in Taipei earlier this year, a gesture that signaled how indispensable the firms are to the global AI ecosystem.

Taiwanese officials will back suppliers that seek to operate in these parks, including by offering loan guarantees and helping communicate with local and federal officials in the US on needs ranging from visas to land, Kung said. Earlier this year, Taiwan pledged to help support US$250 billion in credit guarantees for further investment in the American semiconductor supply chain as part of its trade deal with the US.

Taiwan has already secured a plot of land for an industrial park in Texas, according to a person familiar with the matter. In response, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said it will elaborate on the plan at a suitable time.

See also: Toku lifts revenue growth guidance; expects growth for FY2026 to exceed 20%

Developing a robust supply-chain on US soil has taken on new urgency for Taiwan, which is under pressure to deliver on its investment commitments under the trade deal forged with the Trump administration earlier this year. The self-governing island is also seeking to mitigate the geopolitical risks to its biggest tech manufacturers from long-standing tensions with China.

TSMC alone has pledged to spend US$265 billion to build advanced chipmaking plants in Arizona, the largest-ever foreign investment in America. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s major server assembly partners including Foxconn and Wistron have been expanding their US production capacity to capture growth opportunities from the domestic AI infrastructure buildout.

AI demand is so massive that it’s offering a great opportunity for manufacturers to reshore production to the US, the minister said. Lucrative margins from such business can help cover the high costs initially incurred when building factories in the US, he added, and costs will gradually fall as companies scale up their operations.

At the same time, Taiwanese suppliers are under huge time pressure to fulfill AI orders and are ramping up production both at home and overseas, Kung added. He said that while TSMC is making a major commitment in the US, it’s going to build “many, many more” plants at home. The Taiwanese government isn’t worried about TSMC’s global expansion, which is a move to turn its customers into strategic partners, Kung said.

Texas has become a popular destination for Taiwanese companies after both Foxconn and Wistron recently expanded their presence there.

TSMC said on Thursday it’s also exploring Texas as a new site in the US, although when asked whether the company has decided on the Lone Star state, Kung said the chipmaker is looking at “many locations” for additional investments without elaborating. TSMC declined to comment.

Kung quipped that Tesla Inc CEO Elon Musk, who has vowed to take on TSMC in chipmaking, is welcome to use the new supply chain created by Taiwanese companies in the US, “though we will not completely transfer our technology to him”.
